questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1$ are eigenvalues, and 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$

$$

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable. 

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & ∗ \\ 1 & 0 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the third column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=5,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{3}I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix $M$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix is already  in row echelon form.  It has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.  From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{4}(-2(\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3})-3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 & 1 \\ ∗ & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the first column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -8 & -1 & -3 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-8 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -8 & -1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-8 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}{x}_{3}.$ 
Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4}{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=4,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a+2b=-4+2(4)=4.$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & a & 1 \\ 1 & b & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Computing $A-(-3)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{1}=1.$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 9 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
